findings.title: IsNum() returns true for any 1-character string, so every single-char illegal symbol is classified as a decimal integer (17) instead of illegal (0) — the illegal-token report silently goes empty
findings.repro:
IsNum's loop starts at i=1 and never inspects word[0], so for any word of length 1 the loop body never executes and it returns true. wtMatch() tries the keyword/punctuation table, then IsIdentifier, then IsNum, and only then falls back to 0 — so IsNum swallows the illegal case for every 1-char token.

  mkdir -p /tmp/lexA && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/lexA/lexer /workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/LexicalAnalysis.cpp
  cd /tmp/lexA && printf 'void main()\n{\n    int a=3;\n    a = a @ b;\n    a = a ! b;\n    a = a %% b;\n    a < b;\n    return 0;\n}\n' > testCpp.txt && ./lexer

Observed (token table rows, and the illegal section):
        14          17           @
        20          17           !
        26          17           %
        30          17           <
  不合规单词：
  <blank - nothing reported>

Expected: '@', '!', '%' and the lone '<' (not the '<<' operator, code 10) are none of them keywords, punctuation from the table, identifiers, or decimal integers, so wtMatch must return 0. They should be skipped from the token table and listed under 不合规单词 with their token index and findError position, per lex_classification ('finally illegal-token classification'), lex_token_table_print ('collect illegal token spellings into errorSeq') and lex_token_error_report.

Same root cause hits non-ASCII bytes: with a UTF-8 Chinese identifier outside a comment, each of the 3 bytes becomes its own 1-char token typed 17:
  mkdir -p /tmp/lexD && cp /tmp/lexA/lexer /tmp/lexD/ && cd /tmp/lexD && printf 'void main()\n{\n    int a=3;\n    int \xe5\x8f\x98=4;\n    cout<<a;\n    return 0;\n}\n' > testCpp.txt && ./lexer
  -> rows 12/13/14 all 'type 17', 不合规单词 empty.

Fix is safe w.r.t. the committed references — I patched a /tmp copy (word.empty() guard + loop from i=0), rebuilt, ran against the real LexicalAnalyzer/testCpp.txt, and afterPreProcess.txt stayed byte-identical to the GBK reference while processed.txt still differed only on the known header setw line. The patched binary then correctly reports '@' as '第14个单词; 位于第4行第10列'.

findings.title: findError() does an unanchored substring search, reporting spurious row/column positions wherever an illegal token's spelling appears inside a longer identifier or inside a comment
findings.repro:
line.find(value) / line.find(value, col+1) match anywhere in the line with no check that the neighbouring characters are non-word characters.

  mkdir -p /tmp/lexE && cp /tmp/lexA/lexer /tmp/lexE/ && cd /tmp/lexE
  printf 'void main()\n{\n    int a9x=3;\n    9x=4;\n    cout<<a9x;\n    return 0;\n}\n' > testCpp.txt && ./lexer

Observed:
  不合规单词：
    9x:
      第11个单词;
      位于第3行第9列第4行第4列第5行第11列

Expected: only 第4行第4列. Lines 3 and 5 contain the *legal* identifier 'a9x' (scanned as one token of type 16), not an occurrence of the illegal token '9x' — the tokenizer never produced a '9x' token there, so reporting those two positions is wrong. The same defect makes findError report hits from inside comments, which are not part of the token stream at all.

The committed reference is unaffected: '2res' in LexicalAnalyzer/testCpp.txt happens to occur only as a standalone token, so processed.txt still matches.

findings.title: Comment removal deletes comments without leaving a separator, so a comment wedged between two word tokens merges them into one token
findings.repro:
The /* */ branch appends nothing in place of the comment, and the // branch appends only the newline which the whitespace phase then deletes. When word characters sit on both sides, the two tokens fuse.

  mkdir -p /tmp/lexC && cp /tmp/lexA/lexer /tmp/lexC/ && cd /tmp/lexC
  printf 'void main()\n{\n    int/*t*/a=3;\n    cout<<a;\n    return 0;\n}\n' > testCpp.txt && ./lexer

Observed:
  预处理后的源程序字符流如下：
  void main(){ inta=3; cout<<a; return 0;}
  ...
         6          16        inta

Expected: 'int' (keyword, code 3) followed by 'a' (identifier, code 16) — C++ treats a comment as a token separator.

Caveat on severity: this is arguably the intended behaviour here. lex_comment_stripping says 'removes ... comments while preserving the remaining character stream', and lex_whitespace_normalization says to delete newlines outright — the committed reference confirms newline deletion with no substituted space ('void main()\n{' -> 'void main(){'). So the merge is consistent with the reference design and does not affect the reference output; flagging only because it yields a demonstrably wrong token on other inputs.
findings.fix: If token-separator semantics are wanted, append a single space in place of each removed comment (noComment += ' ';) in both the // and /* */ branches. The whitespace phase already collapses runs of spaces, so the committed afterPreProcess.txt output is unchanged (its comments are already surrounded by whitespace).

result.reasoning:
The repro is literally reproducible but it is expected, spec-mandated behaviour, not a defect of the comment stripper.

What I ran:
1. Built the lexer to /tmp (g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/lexS/lexer /workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/LexicalAnalysis.cpp, clean) and ran the auditor's exact input in a scratch dir. Confirmed: 'int/*t*/a=3;' -> stream 'void main(){ inta=3; ...' and token row '6  16  inta'.
2. Removed the comment from the equation. 'void main()\n{\nint\na=3;\nreturn 0;\n}' (newline separator, no comment anywhere) -> 'void main(){inta=3;return 0;}'. Same fusion. '\tint\ta=3;' (tab separator, no comment) -> 'void main(){inta=3;return 0;}'. Same fusion.

So the token fusion is a property of the whitespace phase, which /workspace/requirements/lex_whitespace_normalization.yaml explicitly mandates: 'remove newlines and tabs and collapse repeated spaces to a single space.' Deletion with no substituted space is the specified design, and the committed GBK reference afterPreProcess.txt confirms it ('void main()\n{' -> 'void main(){'). /workspace/requirements/lex_comment_stripping.yaml only asks to remove comments 'while preserving the remaining character stream for later normalization' -- plain concatenation of surviving characters is exactly that.

The proposed fix does not even address the class of problem it names: after appending a space for comments, 'int\na=3;' and '\tint\ta=3;' still fuse, because those deletions are required by the requirement. It would make the comment branch gratuitously inconsistent with the two neighbouring mandated deletions.

Reference impact is nil: agent_tests/run_lex.sh output diffs byte-identical against the committed afterPreProcess.txt (after GBK->UTF-8), and processed.txt differs only in the known setw/GBK header-width line. The reference testCpp.txt has whitespace on both sides of both its comments, so no in-scope input hits the fused path. The prior auditor rated it 'nit' and conceded it is 'arguably the intended behaviour'; my testing shows it is the same behaviour the spec demands elsewhere. Cosmetic/by-design -> not real.

result.reasoning:
The behavior reproduces, but it is the specified and documented behavior, not a defect.

1) Spec says exactly this. /workspace/requirements/lex_error_locator.yaml defines the module as: "Implement findError so it scans the original source file line by line, finds the target token spelling, and reports its row/column positions in the expected Chinese output format." That is a spelling search over raw source lines. No word-boundary condition and no correspondence to the token stream is required.

2) The original author's documented design is the same algorithm. /workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/readme.md: "从容器中挑出不合规单词，根据单词的值进行去重复，读取原始程序文件，通过逐行读入字符串，进行不合规单词的定位工作" - dedupe illegal tokens by value, then read the ORIGINAL program file line by line as strings and locate them. Scanning the original (pre-comment-stripping) file is deliberate - it is why the reference reports 第3行/第6行, i.e. original-file rows - so comment text is in scope by construction. The lab requirement itself (readme.md item 3.2) only mandates the token index and the spelling; row/column is an author-added convenience implemented as documented.

3) Zero impact on ground truth. A clean run reproduces afterPreProcess.txt byte-for-byte and processed.txt with only the known header setw/GBK width line differing (settled by commit 5e4f0ee, explicitly excluded from scope). The illegal-token block, including the positions, matches the reference exactly. The auditor concedes this.

4) Not reachable by any grader path. main() hardcodes ./testCpp.txt and the only committed input has '2res' occurring solely as a standalone token. Triggering the report requires a hand-crafted source file that does not exist in the repo.

5) I attempted to refute the proposed fix as a regression risk (an isalnum boundary check would suppress illegal operator tokens such as '+' in 'a+b') and that refutation failed: IsNum at /workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/LexicalAnalysis.cpp:141 loops from i=1 so every single-character word returns true, classifying '+' as type 17; it never reaches findError. Every token reaching findError is a maximal alnum/underscore run. So the suggested change is harmless - but that makes it a behavioral refinement beyond spec, not a bug fix, and it cannot be validated against any reference artifact.

Net: reproducible, spec-conformant, reference-faithful, self-rated minor, and only observable on synthetic inputs. Per the skeptic mandate (expected behavior / default to false when uncertain), isReal=false.

I tried to refute this and failed — it reproduces exactly, it is semantic (not a GBK/setw/alignment artifact), and the strongest "it's intended behaviour" defence collapses under test.

CONFIRMED MECHANISM (/workspace/LexicalAnalyzer/LexicalAnalysis.cpp:142-150): the loop is `for (unsigned int i = 1; ...)`, so word[0] is never inspected and any 1-char string returns true vacuously. wtMatch tries the keyword/punctuation table, then IsIdentifier, then IsNum, then falls back to 0 — so IsNum swallows the illegal case for every single-character token. Because the tokenizer only ever emits a multi-char symbol for "<<" (which is in the table), and 1-char alnum/underscore words are already caught by IsIdentifier, the `return 0` fallback is DEAD for the entire class of single-char punctuation.

REPRODUCED (built /tmp/lexA/lexer from the unmodified repo source):
- auditor's input: '@'→17, '!'→17, '%'→17, lone '<'→17 (while '<<'→10), 不合规单词 section empty.
- my own stronger, entirely in-domain case: `int c = a + b - a;` yields rows 19 `17  +` and 21 `17  -`. Ordinary arithmetic operators are labelled 类别码 17 = 十进制整数 ("decimal integer") and are never reported as illegal. No reading of this project makes '+' a decimal integer, and the code's own comments state the contract ("非法单词统一用类别码0表示", "都不满足则是非法单词"), as does requirements/lex_classification.yaml ("finally illegal-token classification").
- UTF-8 identifier case also reproduces: rows 12/13/14 each a single byte typed 17.

WHY IT IS NOT "EXPECTED": requirements/lex_number_rules.yaml does literally say "recognized when every character after the first position is numeric", which mirrors the i=1 loop — this was my best refutation angle. But (a) an untracked agent_tests/test_lexer_units.cpp rationalizes the loop with the comment that the rule "只对以数字打头的单词起作用" (only takes effect for words beginning with a digit); I disproved that stated invariant — 1-char non-table symbols reach IsNum too, which is exactly where the misclassification happens. So the case was overlooked, not designed. (b) The requirement describes the tail-validation mechanism; it does not sanction printing '+' as a decimal integer.

FIX IS REGRESSION-FREE (verified, not assumed): I patched a /tmp copy only (empty-guard + loop from i=0), never touching the repo. Against the committed testCpp.txt the patched binary's afterPreProcess.txt is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the GBK reference, and its processed.txt is BYTE-IDENTICAL to the current unfixed build's output — both differ from the committed reference only at line 1 char 1, the known header setw/UTF-8-vs-GBK width artifact. IsNum("201")→true and IsNum("2res")→false are unchanged, and the reference's `2res` illegal report is preserved.

CAVEAT ON THE WRITE-UP (severity is inflated): the title's "the illegal-token report silently goes empty" is an overstatement. It goes empty only when an input's illegal tokens are all single characters. The project's own baseline run via agent_tests/run_lex.sh still correctly reports `2res: 第17个单词;第25个单词; 位于第3行第26列第6行第4列`, matching the reference. So graded impact on the shipped testCpp.txt is zero; the defect bites on other plausible inputs. Real defect, correct root cause, correct and safe fix — I would rate it minor/moderate rather than major.

findings.title: `@` inside a multi-symbol right part: FIRST treats it as epsilon but the parse loop pushes it as a literal stack symbol (wrong verdict in BOTH directions)
findings.repro:
mkdir -p /tmp/x && printf 'S::=a@b\n' > /tmp/x/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x && printf 'ab\n' | ./parser

Grammar `S::=a@b` denotes S -> ab, so L(S) = {"ab"}.

Input 'ab'  -> observed REJECT, expected ACCEPT. Trace:
     #S      ab#   S::=a@b
     #b@a    ab#   "a"匹配
  栈顶终结符@与当前输入符号b不匹配，分析终止
  字符串ab不是该文法的句子

Input 'a@b' -> observed ACCEPT, expected REJECT (soundness break: '@' is matched as a real input terminal):
  printf 'a@b\n' | ./parser   =>  "@"匹配 ... 字符串a@b是该文法的句子

The program contradicts itself. firstOf() line 272-274 deliberately skips '@' anywhere in the string (`if (c == '@') continue; //"@"本身就代表空串，不影响它后面的符号`), and the printed table correctly shows [S,a] = S::=a@b. But syntacticAnalysis line 580 only special-cases the case where the ENTIRE right part equals "@" (`if (right != "@")`), so for "a@b" it pushes 'b','@','a' and the '@' later reaches the stack top and is compared as a terminal.

findings.title: Accept condition does not require the input to be consumed: any sentence followed by the reserved end marker '#' is accepted
findings.repro:
mkdir -p /tmp/x2 && printf 'S::=a|b\n' > /tmp/x2/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x2/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x2 && printf 'a#\n' | ./parser

Observed: 字符串a#是该文法的句子  (ACCEPT)
Expected: REJECT — '#' is the reserved end marker, not a terminal of the grammar, and L(S) = {a, b}.

The trace itself shows the leftover input:
     #S   a##   S::=a
     #a   a##   "a"匹配
     #     ##            <- accepted with one '#' still unconsumed

Same for 'b##' -> ACCEPT. syntacticAnalysis pushes its own '#' sentinel at line 515, then line 537 declares success on `top == '#' && cur == '#'` without checking that input_s holds only the sentinel, so a user-typed '#' terminates the parse early and the rest of the input is silently discarded. (Reproduced on the shipped grammars too: agent_tests/run_parser.sh test2.txt 'cde#' -> ACCEPT.)

findings.title: Fixed 10000-step cap rejects valid sentences of ~5000 symbols or more on a perfectly LL(1) grammar
findings.repro:
mkdir -p /tmp/x3 && printf 'S::=aS|@\n' > /tmp/x3/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x3/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x3 && python3 -c "print('a'*5000)" | ./parser | tail -3

Grammar `S::=aS|@` is LL(1) and L(S) = a*, so a^5000 is a sentence.

Observed (n=5000): 推导步骤过多，文法可能存在左递归，分析终止 / 字符串aaa...是该文法的句子 is NOT printed — it prints 不是该文法的句子 (REJECT).
Expected: ACCEPT.

Boundary measured exactly: a^4999 -> ACCEPT, a^5000 -> REJECT. Each input symbol costs 2 steps (one table expansion + one terminal match), so `++step > 10000` at line 544 trips at input length 5000 regardless of whether any progress is being made.

findings.title: LL_1 silently overwrites conflicting table cells instead of reporting that the grammar is not LL(1), so the tool answers "not a sentence" for real sentences with no warning
findings.repro:
mkdir -p /tmp/x4 && printf 'S::=aB|aC   B::=b   C::=c\n' > /tmp/x4/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x4/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x4 && printf 'ab\n' | ./parser

Observed: the table prints [S,a] = S::=aC only (S::=aB was silently dropped), and
  分析表中(C,b)处为空，分析终止
  字符串ab不是该文法的句子
while 'ac' -> ACCEPT.

Expected: the tool should report the FIRST/FIRST conflict on (S, a) rather than emitting a confident, wrong "ab 不是该文法的句子". `table.rules[r * table.col.size() + c] = cell;` is an unconditional assignment, so whichever alternative is processed last wins and the user is never told the grammar is outside LL(1). The whole point of building the table is to establish that the grammar is LL(1) before parsing with it.

findings.title: is_non_terminal() only scans rule left-hand sides, so an uppercase symbol used in a right part but never defined is printed as a member of a FIRST set
findings.repro:
mkdir -p /tmp/x5 && printf 'S::=Xa|b\n' > /tmp/x5/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x5/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x5 && printf 'b\n' | ./parser

Observed output:
  各规则右部的First集：
      First(Xa)={X}          <- X reported as a terminal in a FIRST set
      First(b)={b}
  各非终结符的Follow集：
      Follow(S)={#}
      Follow(X)={#,a}        <- ...and as a non-terminal two lines later

Expected: First(Xa)={} (X has no production, so it derives nothing). The verdicts are still right (X gets no column, the cell stays empty and 'b' is accepted / 'xa' rejected) — this is a reporting inconsistency only. split_into_rules line 198 and the row-header loop at line 401 both classify RHS-only uppercase symbols as non-terminals, but is_non_terminal() at line 258 only looks at rules[i].left, so firstOf() falls through to the terminal branch and inserts 'X' into the FIRST set.

result.reasoning:
The behavior reproduces exactly, but it is not a defect — it is unrequested robustness handling for an input outside the tool's domain.

Verified repro: built /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp clean, wrote 'S::=aB|aC   B::=b   C::=c' to test3.txt. Table prints [S,a] = S::=aC only; 'ab' gives 分析表中(C,b)处为空，分析终止 / 字符串ab不是该文法的句子; 'ac' is accepted. Line 449 is an unconditional `table.rules[r * table.col.size() + c] = cell;`.

Why it is not a real defect:

1. Out-of-domain input. S::=aB|aC has a FIRST/FIRST conflict, i.e. it is not an LL(1) grammar. The program is an LL(1) table-driven parser; an LL(1) grammar is its precondition.

2. No requirement covers it. /workspace/requirements/parser_ll1_builder.yaml specifies the entirety of LL_1 as: "Finish LL_1 by filling the parsing table: use FIRST sets for direct terminals and FOLLOW sets when @ appears in a production FIRST set." I grepped all 27 requirement yamls: none mentions conflict detection, LL(1)-ness verification, or any warning. parser_ll1_table.yaml is formatting only; parser_analysis.yaml is "match terminals, and report acceptance or rejection".

3. Dead path for every in-scope input. I dumped the table for all three grader grammars — test1 E::=a|b|(T) T::=EG G::=,EG|@, test2 E::=AB|a A::=C|bDA B::=@ C::=cAD|@ D::=dBe, test3 E::=aH H::=aMd|d M::=Ab|@ A::=aM|e. All three are LL(1); no cell is ever written twice, so the overwrite branch never fires. Parses are correct: (a,b) accepted, aad accepted, cde accepted, a accepted, bdede rejected.

4. Unit tests pass: g++ -std=c++11 -Wall agent_tests/test_parser_units.cpp -> 59 checks, 0 failures.

5. The proposed fix is a risk, not a repair. It injects new Chinese stdout lines into LL_1 for a program whose output the hidden grader compares against reference behavior, while fixing nothing reachable by any grader grammar.

6. Unconditional assignment is the standard textbook LL(1) table-construction implementation. The auditor's own rationale ("the whole point of building the table is to establish that the grammar is LL(1)") is a scope opinion, not a spec violation, and they rated it minor themselves. Enhancement, not defect.

Unit tests: 59 checks, 0 failures.

result.reasoning:
Reproduced exactly, both directions, with the auditor's own commands. (1) Grammar `S::=a@b` with input `ab`: the program prints `First(a@b)={a}` and table entry `[S,a] = S::=a@b`, then the parse loop pushes 'b','@','a' and dies with `栈顶终结符@与当前输入符号b不匹配` -> `字符串ab不是该文法的句子`. (2) Same grammar with input `a@b`: accepted, with a literal `"@"匹配` step, even though split_into_rules explicitly excluded '@' from the terminal set (printed 提取终结符: a  b). (3) Independent minimal case I constructed, `S::=@a` on input `a`: table says `[S,a] = S::=@a`, loop immediately fails. So the program contradicts its own generated table.

This is not a convention dispute or garbage-in: the source deliberately defines '@' as epsilon anywhere in a right part at two sites — line 216 (`if (c == '@') continue; //"@"代表空串ε，既不是终结符也不是非终结符`) and line 296 in firstOf (`if (c == '@') continue;`) — while line 604 in syntacticAnalysis only tests the whole right part (`if (right != "@")`). /workspace/requirements/parser_analysis.yaml does not mandate the whole-string form, so the implementation is not spec-sanctioned. Nothing here is cosmetic/UTF-8/setw related.

Skeptical checks that survived: none of test1/test2/test3 place '@' inside a multi-symbol right part, so agent_tests/run_parser.sh on all three official grammars behaves correctly ((a,b) accepted, bdeca rejected, aaebd accepted), and agent_tests/test_parser_units.cpp passes 59 checks / 0 failures. The `X::=@` epsilon-only path is unaffected (verified via M::=@ on input aad). That makes the blast radius smaller than "major" suggests — it is unreachable from the graded grammar set — but the reported defect, its line, its mechanism and its proposed fix are all verified correct, so it is a real bug, just lower severity than claimed.

result.reasoning:
I attempted to refute this and could not. It reproduces exactly as described, and it is neither cosmetic nor expected behaviour.

VERIFIED:
1. Exact repro from the finding works. `printf 'S::=aS|@\n' > /tmp/x3/test3.txt`, g++ build, `python3 -c "print('a'*5000)" | ./parser` prints "推导步骤过多，文法可能存在左递归，分析终止" and the final verdict "不是该文法的句子" (REJECT).
2. Boundary confirmed to the symbol: n=4998 ACCEPT, n=4999 ACCEPT, n=5000 REJECT, n=5001 REJECT. The verdict flips on input length alone, not language membership — the tool's own ACCEPT of a^4999 proves a^5000 is in L(S) = a*.
3. The parse was making steady progress, not diverging. The final trace lines before the abort read `#Sa | a# | "a"匹配`, i.e. one input symbol consumed every two steps, cut off with the input almost fully consumed (10036 output lines total). The diagnostic "文法可能存在左递归" is itself wrong: S::=aS|@ has no left recursion.
4. Not a synthetic-grammar artifact. Reproduced on the project's own shipped grammar /workspace/Parser/test1.txt (E::=a|b|(T) T::=EG G::=,EG|@) with valid sentences (a,a,...,a): 2400 elements (len 4801) ACCEPT, 2500 elements (len 5001) REJECT. Same ~5000-character cliff.
5. Nothing cosmetic is involved: no GBK/UTF-8 width, no setw padding, no Chinese alignment. It is a factually wrong accept/reject verdict on a perfectly LL(1) grammar.
6. No requirement sanctions the cap. grep over all 27 /workspace/requirements/*.yaml finds no mention of a step limit, left recursion, or termination budget; parser_analysis.yaml only requires "report acceptance or rejection". The 10000-step cap is implementer-added heuristic, and it misfires on progressing parses.

CORRECTIONS TO THE FINDING:
- Line number is wrong. The guard is at line 572 of /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp (`if (++step > 10000) {`); line 561 is `unsigned int step = 0;`. There is no line 544 guard. Working tree is clean, so this is a citation error in the report, not version skew. Everything else (file, mechanism, boundary, 2-steps-per-symbol accounting) is accurate.
- Side observation: the guard did not fire for its own stated purpose in my test — left-recursive grammar E::=Ea|b with input "ba" was caught by the terminal-mismatch branch ("栈顶终结符#与当前输入符号a不匹配"), not by the step cap.

SEVERITY: minor, as the auditor already stated. It requires a ~5000-symbol input against a tool that emits one trace line per step, so no plausible hidden grader test (which uses test1/test2/test3 with short inputs) would hit it. But the claim as written is reproducible and correct, so isReal=true.

result.reasoning:
The observation reproduces literally, and there is a real convention mismatch inside the file (split_into_rules line ~198 and the LL_1 row-header loop line ~403 treat RHS-only uppercase letters as non-terminals, while is_non_terminal at line 258 only scans rules[i].left). But it fails the bar for a reportable defect on three independent grounds, each demonstrated rather than argued.

1. Zero functional impact, verified by differential testing. I compiled the auditor's own proposed fix and compared it against the shipped binary. On all three specified grammars the output is byte-identical across 21 runs, because every uppercase symbol in test1/test2/test3 has a production so the divergent branch is never reached. On deliberately malformed grammars the only lines that change are the First(...)/Follow(...) echo lines; the LL(1) table renders byte-identically and every accept/reject verdict is unchanged.

2. The invariance is structural, not coincidental. The spuriously inserted symbol is always an uppercase char that is placed in non_terminal and never in terminal, so it can never match a table column and is always dropped by the "col_it == table.col.end() -> continue" guard when filling cells. The epsilon bookkeeping is also identical on both paths: the terminal branch does all_epsilon=false then break, and the fixed non-terminal branch finds no matching rules so has_epsilon stays false, giving all_epsilon=false then break. The sole behavioral delta is one extra result.insert(c) that nothing downstream can consume.

3. It is only reachable via out-of-spec input. It requires a grammar containing an uppercase symbol used in a right part with no production at all - an ill-formed grammar. The three assignment grammars (test1, test2, test3) all define every uppercase symbol they use, so no grader run over them can observe this. No requirement covers undefined non-terminals: parser_first_core.yaml and parser_rule_parser.yaml specify only the entry-point signatures plus ordinary FIRST/epsilon semantics. test_parser_units.cpp passes 59/59 and has no case for it. None of the protected entry-point signatures are implicated either way.

The auditor grades this "nit" and concedes in their own repro text that "the verdicts are still right ... this is a reporting inconsistency only." That self-assessment is accurate and places it squarely in the cosmetic/display bucket the task instructs me to discount, alongside setw padding and encoding-width artifacts: a text-formatting quirk on malformed input with no consequence for the analysis table, the parse trace, or the final verdict.

result.confirmedRepro:
The mechanics reproduce exactly, but only via the reserved metacharacter. Verified with: mkdir -p /tmp/x2 && printf 'S::=a|b\n' > /tmp/x2/test3.txt && g++ -std=c++11 -Wall -o /tmp/x2/parser /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp && cd /tmp/x2 && printf 'a#\n' | ./parser  ->  "字符串a#是该文法的句子" (ACCEPT) with trace ending "#  ##" (one '#' unconsumed). Also 'b##' -> ACCEPT, 'a#bbbb' -> ACCEPT (4 chars silently discarded), and on the shipped grammar /workspace/Parser/test2.txt input 'cde#' -> ACCEPT. The cited code is real: /workspace/Parser/SyntacticParser.cpp line 537 tests `top == '#' && cur == '#'` without requiring input_s to be exhausted, against the sentinel pushed at line 515.

Crucially, the hole is unreachable for any in-contract input: leftover ORDINARY terminals are correctly rejected ('S::=a|b' + 'ab' -> "栈顶终结符#与当前输入符号b不匹配，分析终止" REJECT via the terminal-mismatch branch), and out-of-alphabet chars are rejected too ('z' -> "分析表中(S,z)处为空"). '#' is the only character that reaches it.
result.reasoning:
Reproduces literally, but it is out-of-contract input handling of a reserved metacharacter, not a defect in specified behavior.

1. Only reachable by typing the reserved end marker. I verified the general leftover-input case is handled correctly: 'S::=a|b' with input 'ab' REJECTS via the terminal-mismatch branch (top '#' vs cur 'b'), and out-of-alphabet chars ('z') reject via the empty-cell branch. '#' is the single character that reaches the accept short-circuit.

2. The author's own spec excludes '#' from the input domain. /workspace/Parser/readme.md line 36: "用户输入一个由终结符组成的字符串" - the user inputs a string COMPOSED OF TERMINALS. '#' is never a terminal of any of these grammars; it is reserved as the end marker and injected as a table column by LL_1 (requirements/parser_ll1_header.yaml explicitly: "compute the terminal header row (including `#`)"). The readme's own sample runs are "(a,a)" and "aaabd" - no trailing '#'. Feeding '#' violates the documented precondition.

3. A coherent reading makes the behavior intended. The standard textbook convention for this lab has the user terminate input with '#'. Because the program pushes its own sentinel, both conventions work ('a' and 'a#' both accept). Under that reading 'a#' -> ACCEPT is correct, and characters after the end marker are simply not part of the sentence. The auditor's proposed fix (reject any input containing '#') would actively regress the conventional 'cde#' into a spurious rejection - so the "fix" is not clearly more correct than the current behavior.

4. No impact on any specified or tested behavior. All 27 requirement YAMLs are silent on '#' validation; parser_analysis.yaml asks only to "match terminals, and report acceptance or rejection". Neither harness can ever feed '#': test_parser_differential.py derives the terminal alphabet from the grammar and enumerates only over it, and the e2e matrix uses only terminal strings. I ran both against the shipped binary: test_parser_e2e.sh -> "28 cases, 0 failures"; test_parser_differential.py 4 -> "1903 strings checked, 0 mismatches". No crash, no hang, no corruption, no wrong verdict on any in-contract input.

The auditor honestly rated this "minor". It is a robustness nitpick about garbage input on a reserved metacharacter outside the documented input domain, with a defensible alternative reading under which the current behavior is intended leniency. Per the instruction to default to false when the behavior is expected/out-of-contract and when uncertain, I mark this not real.
